title: The Merchant's Ledger
subject: Excel
intro: Tove's ledger is a mess and Hrolf the tax collector arrives at sundown. Rebuild the books with real formulas, win the restock gamble, then survive the audit.

objectives.label: Find values by their cell address
Build formulas that calculate from cells and fill down
Choose and use SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX on ranges
Know when to fix a reference with $
Use your calculations to make and explain a decision

badge.name: Ledger Keeper
badge.description: Rebuilt a trading ledger with working formulas and passed the tax collector's audit.

takeaway: Formulas refer to cells, not typed numbers, so they update when the data changes. Ranges feed SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX; $ fixes a reference when you fill down; and Excel does * and / before + and −. When a ledger looks wrong, diagnose before you fix — then let the numbers decide.

scenes.title: The harbour market
scenes.speaker: tove
lines: Pathfinder! Thank the tides. My ledger is a wreck: blank totals, wrong taxes, numbers I just guessed.
See my scales? They tip whenever the ledger is wrong. Hrolf the tax collector arrives at sundown, and he checks every coin.
Help me rebuild the books — properly, with formulas — and you'll share in the profits.

scenes.title: Where is the honey?
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Every cell has an address: its column letter, then its row number.
scenes.code:
A        B       C
1  Item     Price   Qty sold
2  Furs       25       6
3  Honey       8      15
4  Amber      40       3
5  Rope        5      22
scenes.prompt: A customer wants the honey price. Which cell holds it?

options.feedback: Yes. Price is column B and Honey is on row 3, so B3 holds 8.
C3 is Honey's quantity sold (15). Price is in column B.
B2 is the price of Furs. Honey is one row down.
A3 holds the word Honey itself. The price is to its right.

hints: Column letter first, then row number.
Find the Price column, then go down to Honey's row.
scenes.explanation: A cell address is column letter + row number, like B3. Formulas use these addresses to read values.

scenes.title: Balance the scales
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Revenue is price times quantity. Build it once in D2 — the ledger fills it down to D5 like Excel's fill handle.
scenes.prompt: Build the revenue formula for Furs in D2 from the fragments on the bench.
scenes.successFeedback: All four revenues are right: 150, 120, 120 and 110. The scales settle.
hints: Formulas start with =, then use cell addresses instead of numbers.
Furs' price is in B2 and its quantity in C2. Multiply them with *.
scenes.explanation: =B2*C2 multiplies two cells. Filled down, Excel shifts the row numbers (B3*C3, B4*C4…), which is why referring to cells beats typing numbers.

scenes.title: Fill the coin chest
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Now the number that matters most: everything I took in this week.
scenes.prompt: Build a formula in D6 that totals the revenue in D2 to D5.
scenes.successFeedback: 500 silver in the chest this week.
hints: SUM adds up a range of cells.
A range is written first:last, like D2:D5. Don't include the total cell itself.
scenes.explanation: =SUM(D2:D5) adds every cell from D2 to D5. If a sale is corrected, the total updates by itself, unlike =150+120+120+110.

scenes.title: The typical price
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: A sailor asks what my goods cost on average. Not the total — the typical price.
scenes.prompt: Build a formula in B6 for the average price of the four items.
hints: There's a function named after exactly what you want.
AVERAGE of the price column, B2 to B5.
scenes.explanation: AVERAGE adds a range and divides by how many numbers it contains. Choosing the right range matters as much as the right function.

scenes.title: The rune of the greatest
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: The rune-stone by my stall hides the name of a function. Guess it in six tries — real Excel functions only.
scenes.prompt: Which function finds the most expensive item on the stall?
scenes.clue: It looks along a range and returns the largest number. Its opposite finds the smallest.
hints: It's three letters long and stands for 'maximum'.
M _ X
scenes.explanation: MAX returns the largest number in a range; MIN returns the smallest. Both skip text, so a header won't confuse them.

scenes.title: The prize of the stall
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: The most precious item goes at the front of the stall. Use the rune you just uncovered.
scenes.prompt: Build a formula in B6 that returns the highest price.
scenes.successFeedback: 40 silver: the amber takes pride of place.
hints: You want the largest value in the price column.
=MAX(B2:B5)
scenes.explanation: MAX looks through the range and returns the largest number: 40, the amber.

scenes.title: The vanishing tax
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: The harbour tax rate sits in E2. I typed =B2*E2 in C2 and filled it down. Furs are taxed, but everything else shows 0.
scenes.prompt: Diagnose what went wrong, then repair the formula in C2 (it is filled down to C5).

diagnoses.text: Filling down moved E2 to E3, E4, E5 — which are empty
diagnoses.feedback: That's the cause: relative references move when filled.
Tax is revenue times the rate, so * is right. Look at how the formula changes from row to row.

diagnoses.text: The rate in E2 is wrong
diagnoses.feedback: E2 is fine — Furs get the right tax. The other rows aren't reading E2 at all.
SUM adds up ranges; this is one revenue times one rate. The reference is the problem.

scenes.successFeedback: Every row now uses the rate in E2: 15, 12, 12 and 11.
hints: Fill the formula down in your head: what does E2 become on row 3?
Lock the rate with $ so it stays at E2: $E$2.
scenes.explanation: Relative references (E2) shift when filled; absolute references ($E$2) don't. Use $ for single settings like a tax rate that every row shares.

scenes.title: The impossible losses
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: My profit column says I lose 83 silver on furs. Profit should be (price − cost) × quantity. Someone wrote =B2-C2*D2.
scenes.prompt: Diagnose the bug and repair E2 (filled down to E5).

diagnoses.text: Excel multiplies before it subtracts, so it did 25 − (18 × 6)
The cell references point at the wrong columns
diagnoses.feedback: B, C and D are the right cells. The order Excel works in is the problem.
Each row should use its own price and cost, so no $ is needed here.
The data is fine. The same numbers give a sensible profit when the formula is right.

hints: Which happens first in Excel, − or *?
Brackets make the subtraction happen first: (B2-C2)*D2.
scenes.explanation: Excel does * and / before + and −. Brackets change the order: =(B2-C2)*D2 subtracts first, then multiplies.

scenes.title: The cursed runes
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: These cursed runes appeared in my old ledger. Each one is Excel telling you something specific.
scenes.prompt: Match each error rune to what caused it.

right.text: Dividing by zero or an empty cell
Arithmetic on text, like =A2*2 when A2 says Furs
A reference to cells that were deleted

feedback.div0: #DIV/0! is about division: something divided by 0 or by an empty cell.
feedback.name: #NAME? means Excel doesn't recognise a word — usually a typo in a function name.
feedback.value: #VALUE! appears when a calculation is fed text instead of a number.
feedback.ref: #REF! means a reference no longer points anywhere, often after deleting rows or columns.

scenes.successFeedback: The curse is lifted: you can read Excel's error runes.
hints: Read each error's name literally.
#NAME? is about names Excel doesn't recognise; #REF! is about references.
scenes.explanation: Errors are messages, not failures: each names the kind of problem, so you know where to look.

scenes.title: The rune wheel
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Sailors spin this wheel for luck. Here it tests memory: it lands on a rune you've already learned — in a new place on the island. Stake XP if you're confident.
scenes.prompt: Spin the wheel, then solve the challenge it lands on.

segments.label: Σ SUM

challenge.prompt: The crew's weekly wages are in B2:B5. Build the total in B6.

hints: A total of a range is a job for SUM.
=SUM(B2:B5)
segments.explanation: SUM works the same on wages as on revenue: a range in, one total out.

segments.label: x̄ AVERAGE

challenge.prompt: Sigrun's daily fish catch is in B2:B5. Build the typical daily catch in B6.

hints: 'Typical' here means the mean.
=AVERAGE(B2:B5)
segments.explanation: AVERAGE gives the typical value of a range — fish, prices or anything else.

segments.label: ▲ MAX

challenge.prompt: Crate weights are in B2:B7. Which formula finds the heaviest crate?

options.feedback: Yes: MAX returns the largest value.
MIN finds the lightest crate.
SUM gives the total weight of all crates.
COUNT tells you how many crates there are.

hints: Heaviest means largest.
The function you uncovered on the rune-stone.
segments.explanation: MAX finds the largest value whether it's a price or a weight.

segments.label: $ LOCK

challenge.prompt: A trader converts prices in column B with the exchange rate in E1, and will fill the formula down. Which version keeps working on every row?

options.feedback: Right: $E$1 stays put while B2 moves to B3, B4…
Filled down, E1 drifts to E2, E3… and the rate disappears.
Now every row converts the same price, B2.
It works today, but the rate is hidden in every formula; change it once in E1 instead.

hints: Which part must move as you fill down, and which must stay?
Lock only the rate.
segments.explanation: Lock single settings with $; leave the row's own values relative.

segments.label: ( ) ORDER

challenge.prompt: Tobin bets Tove that =10+2*3 makes 36. What does Excel return?

options.feedback: Yes: 2*3 first, then add 10.
That's left-to-right reading. Excel multiplies before it adds.
Check again: only 2 and 3 are multiplied.
It's a valid formula; Excel just follows its order of operations.

hints: Excel doesn't read left to right.
Multiplication before addition.
segments.explanation: * and / come before + and −; use brackets when you mean otherwise.

segments.label: ⌖ CELL

challenge.code:
A        B       C
1  Ship     Crew    Cargo
2  Raven      12      40
3  Wolf        9      65
4  Gull       15      30
challenge.prompt: Which cell holds the Wolf's cargo?

options.feedback: Yes: Cargo is column C, Wolf is row 3.
B3 is the Wolf's crew.
C2 is the Raven's cargo.
Excel writes the column letter first: C3.

hints: Column letter first, then row number.
Cargo is column C.
segments.explanation: Addresses work the same on every sheet: column letter, then row number.

hints: Read the challenge the wheel landed on carefully.
scenes.explanation: Recall in a new setting is how skills stick.

scenes.title: The restock gamble
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: The supply ship is in. I have 200 silver. Whatever I order, I pay for — but I can only sell as many as customers want (the Demand column). MIN(D2,E2) picks the smaller of demand and order.
scenes.prompt: Write the profit formula for F2 (filled down), then set the orders. Tove needs at least 165 silver profit without overspending.
scenes.successFeedback: The ship sails off and the chest is heavier.
hints: Profit = what you earn from sales − what you paid. Sales are capped by demand: MIN(D2,E2) units.
=B2*MIN(D2,E2)-C2*E2. Then compare how much profit each item makes per silver spent.
scenes.explanation: A good model separates what you sell (price × MIN(demand, order)) from what you pay (cost × order). Over-ordering never earns more — it only adds cost.

scenes.title: Why the rope rotted
scenes.speaker: tove
scenes.context: Last season I ordered 30 coils of rope for 2 silver each. Customers wanted 22. I sold them at 5.
scenes.prompt: What does the ledger say happened, and why?

options.text: Profit was 50: 22 sold for 110, but all 30 cost 60. The 8 unsold coils lost 16.
options.feedback: Exactly: 5 × 22 − 2 × 30 = 50. Ordering to demand (22) would have made 66.

options.text: Profit was 90: more stock always means more profit.
options.feedback: Only 22 sold. 5 × 30 − 2 × 30 = 90 counts sales that never happened.

options.text: Profit was 66 either way: unsold rope costs nothing.
options.feedback: Unsold rope was still paid for: 8 × 2 = 16 silver gone.

options.text: It was a loss, because cost is more than demand.
options.feedback: Cost (2) and demand (22) aren't comparable. Work out sales and costs separately.

hints: Sales are limited by demand: 22 coils.
scenes.explanation: Numbers become decisions when you can say what they mean: unsold stock is pure cost.

scenes.title: Sundown: the audit
scenes.speaker: hrolf
lines: So. You are the Pathfinder who has been 'fixing' this ledger.
I bring my own figures. I check every formula, and I don't give hints for free.
Pass my audit and the Jarl's Great Hall opens to you. Fail, and you can try again — but my numbers will change.

scenes.title: Audit I: Hrolf's figures
scenes.speaker: hrolf
scenes.context: My ledger puts quantity before price. Revenue for every row, from one formula.
scenes.prompt: Build the revenue formula in D2. It is filled down to D5.
hints: Same idea as before, columns in a different order.
Quantity × price, using this row's cells.
scenes.explanation: Formulas follow the meaning of the columns, not their position — read the headers first.

scenes.title: Audit II: the short tax
scenes.speaker: hrolf
scenes.context: Your total tax is short. I count the tax on all four items. The rate is in D2.
scenes.prompt: Diagnose the fault in B6 and repair it.

diagnoses.text: The range stops at B4, so Rope is left out
diagnoses.feedback: Yes: B2:B4 covers three items, not four.
This formula isn't filled anywhere, so D2 can't drift. Count the rows in the range.
SUM( ) is worked out first anyway. Look at which rows the range includes.
The rate is fine; the total it's applied to is too small.

hints: How many items does B2:B4 cover?
The range must run to the last item, B5.
scenes.explanation: A range that stops one row short is the most common SUM bug. Check the first and last cell every time.

scenes.title: Audit III: the missing coins
scenes.speaker: hrolf
scenes.context: My men counted the coins for each item. One item's coins don't match what the ledger says it sold. Find it.
scenes.prompt: Which item's coins don't match price × quantity sold?

options.feedback: Check it: work out price × quantity for furs and compare it with the coins counted.
Check it: work out price × quantity for honey and compare it with the coins counted.
Check it: work out price × quantity for amber and compare it with the coins counted.
Check it: work out price × quantity for rope and compare it with the coins counted.

hints: Expected coins = Price × Qty sold, row by row.
Compare each product with the Coins counted column.
scenes.explanation: Reconciling expected against actual, row by row, is how real audits find missing money.

scenes.title: Audit IV: Hrolf's riddle
scenes.speaker: hrolf
scenes.context: Answer my riddle. Real function names only.
scenes.clue: Not the total, not the greatest: I want the typical price — add them up and share them out evenly.
hints: Seven letters.
It begins with A.
scenes.explanation: AVERAGE = SUM ÷ COUNT: the typical value of a range.

scenes.title: Audit V: the verdict
scenes.speaker: hrolf
scenes.context: Next season the Jarl allows only three goods per stall. Here is what each earned and what its stock cost.
scenes.prompt: Which good should Tove drop, and why?

options.text: Furs — the lowest profit (revenue − stock cost)
options.feedback: Compute revenue − stock cost for every good before deciding.

options.text: Honey — the lowest profit (revenue − stock cost)
options.feedback: Compute revenue − stock cost for every good before deciding.

options.text: Amber — the lowest profit (revenue − stock cost)
options.feedback: Compute revenue − stock cost for every good before deciding.

options.text: Rope — the lowest profit (revenue − stock cost)
options.feedback: Compute revenue − stock cost for every good before deciding.

hints: High revenue isn't the same as high profit.
Profit = Revenue − Stock cost for each row; drop the smallest.
scenes.explanation: Decide on profit, not revenue: a good that sells a lot can still earn the least.

scenes.title: The audit is passed
scenes.speaker: tove
lines: Hrolf left without a word — which means the books balance!
Every number in this ledger updates itself now, and I know how to check it.
The Jarl's steward wants someone who can read numbers like that. The Great Hall is waiting.
